migrationNotes: Spine: a star is a car with a fuel tank and a thirst. We set its fuel against its burn rate, see that mass raises the burn rate faster than the fuel, turn that into a lifetime, and follow the star to what it leaves behind.
Question astro-star-lives-8 is no longer in the lesson; its id and key are unchanged in the question bank.

lesson.title: How mass sets a star's life

lead.text: Take a car with a full tank. How far it goes depends on two things, the size of the tank and how fast the engine drinks. A big tank feeding a thirsty engine can run dry sooner than a small tank feeding a frugal one. The time until empty is the fuel divided by the rate of use.

A star has both. On the main sequence it makes its light by fusion in its core, where hydrogen nuclei are squeezed together hot enough to join into helium and release energy. The hydrogen in the core is the tank. The rate of burning is the star's luminosity, since the energy that leaves as light each second has to come from somewhere.

So the time a star spends on the main sequence, its main-sequence lifetime, is its fuel divided by its luminosity. The Sun's is about 10 billion years. Whether a heavier star lasts longer or shorter depends on how its tank and its burn rate compare, and the next screens measure both.
Use the car idea. The time until the tank is empty is the fuel divided by the rate of burning.

reveal.text: X has more fuel, but it burns it so much faster that it lasts only a quarter as long.

lead.text: Now give the stars different masses. The fuel is the easy part. A star with twice the mass has about twice the hydrogen, so the tank grows in proportion to the mass M, measured in solar masses (M☉).

The burn rate grows far faster. Astronomers have measured the masses and luminosities of many main-sequence stars, and in solar units they follow roughly L = M³·⁵. A star of 3 M☉ shines at about 3³·⁵ = 3³ × √3 = 27 × 1.73 ≈ 47 L☉. The fit is rough, good to about a factor of two, but the steepness is what matters. Tripling the mass multiplies the fuel by 3 and the burn rate by nearly 50.

afterFigure.text: The chart shows the same thing. Moving up the main sequence takes you to heavier stars. The three stars in the picture have about 0.12, 1 and 2 solar masses, and each step up in mass lifts a star far higher on the band.

lead.text: Work it the way the last screen did for 3 M☉: the whole-number part of the power, times a square root for the half.

reveal.text: A 2 M☉ star shines at about 11 L☉, with twice the fuel to feed it. Mass fixes where a main-sequence star sits on the chart.

lead.text: Divide the fuel by the burn rate. The fuel is proportional to M and the burn rate to M³·⁵, so the lifetime is proportional to M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵. The exponent is negative because the burn rate grows faster than the fuel, and a negative exponent makes the lifetime shrink as the mass goes up.
Scale the rule to the Sun, whose lifetime is about 10 billion years: t = 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, or 10 billion years ÷ M²·⁵, with M in solar masses. To work out M²·⁵, take M² and multiply it by √M.

Try it on a few masses. A star of 10 M☉ has M²·⁵ ≈ 316, so it lasts about 32 million years. A star with a quarter of the Sun's mass has M⁻²·⁵ = 4²·⁵ = 32, so the rule gives 320 billion years, far longer than the universe has existed. Red dwarfs, the lightest stars, live so long that none has yet run out of fuel.

steps.headline: Find the main-sequence lifetime of a 2 M☉ star.

workedSteps.text: Work out the power of the mass.
Divide the Sun's lifetime by it.

lead.text: Same rule, a heavier star. Give the answer in millions of years.

reveal.text: A star four times the Sun's mass lasts only about 3% as long. More fuel does not make up for a much faster burn.

lead.text: Astronomers can often tell how long a star can last, for instance by dating the cluster it belongs to, and then want its mass. The rule has to run in reverse. Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵. Take the reciprocal to get M²·⁵, then raise that to the power 1 ÷ 2.5 = 0.4 to get M.

As an example, take a star that lasts one hundredth as long as the Sun. Then M²·⁵ = 100, and M = 100⁰·⁴ = 10⁰·⁸ ≈ 6.3 solar masses. A calculator does the power in one step with its power key. A short-lived star is a heavy one, and the shorter the life, the heavier the star.
Turn the rule round, step by step, as on the last screen.

reveal.text: A star that lasts only 10 million years is about 16 times the Sun's mass. Short lives mean heavy stars.

lead.text: When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the star's time on the main sequence is over. The core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers swell, and the star leaves the band to become a giant. The Sun will do this in about five billion years.

What happens next depends on the star's mass. A star below about 10 M☉ sheds its outer layers and leaves its core as a white dwarf. A star from about 10 to 40 M☉ ends when its core collapses in a violent explosion called a supernova, and leaves a neutron star, a ball of neutrons about 20 km across with more mass than the Sun. Above about 40 M☉ the collapse leaves a black hole, a region where gravity is so strong that the escape speed is higher than the speed of light.

afterFigure.text: These boundaries are approximate. The figure lists the remnant for three masses, and the mass the star starts with is what decides which it becomes.

lead.text: This star is far heavier than the Sun but not among the heaviest. Use the mass boundaries from the last screen.

reveal.text: A star's initial mass decides its remnant. A 15 M☉ star sits in the middle band: its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

lesson.orientation: Estimate main-sequence lifetimes from mass and predict how a star ends.
lesson.reviewLabel: How mass sets a star's life
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with a band of stars across the chart, the main sequence, and the fact that a star's mass decides where on the band it sits. Heavy stars blaze at the top left and light ones glow faintly at the bottom right. Mass also decides something else, which is how long a star lasts.

The Sun has shone for about 4.6 billion years and has about as long again to go. A star ten times as heavy does not last anything like that. It burns out in a few tens of millions of years, which is less time than has passed since the dinosaurs died. That looks backwards, because a heavier star has more fuel to burn.

To see why, think of a car's fuel tank. How far a car goes depends on the size of the tank and on how fast the engine drinks. This lesson treats a star the same way: it sets the star's fuel against its thirst, then follows the star to the end of its life.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate how long a star shines from its mass, and what it leaves behind.

recap.keyIdea: A star's life is fuel divided by burn rate. Mass raises the burn rate faster than the fuel, so t ∝ M⁻²·⁵: heavy stars live short lives, and mass also decides the remnant.

blocks.text: You began with a car's tank and its thirst, and found that a star with 3 times the fuel burning 12 times as fast lasts only a quarter as long. A 4 M☉ star lasts about 312.5 million years, a star that lasts 10 million years has about 16 times the Sun's mass, and a 15 M☉ star leaves a neutron star.

recap.nextHook: Stars live and die inside galaxies, vast islands of stars. The next lesson looks at the light of distant galaxies, whose spectral lines are shifted just as a moving star's are.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence lifetime scales as t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, with M in solar masses. Find the lifetime of a 4 M☉ star in millions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: Raise 4 to the power −2.5.
4²·⁵ is 4² × √4.
Divide 10 billion years by 4²·⁵ and convert to millions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4⁻²·⁵ = 1/32, so t = 10 billion/32 = 0.3125 billion years = 312.5 million years.

questions.onCorrect: 312.5 million years. 4²·⁵ = 32, so the lifetime is a thirty-second of the Sun's.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in billions of years. Convert to millions.
That divides by M alone. The burn rate rises with mass too, so divide by M²·⁵.

questions.prompt: Main-sequence luminosity scales roughly as L ∝ M³·⁵. How many times the Sun's luminosity does a 2 M☉ star have? Give one decimal place.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 2³·⁵ into 2³ × 2⁰·⁵.
Multiply 8 by √2.
questions.onCorrect: 11.3 L☉. 2³·⁵ = 2³ × √2: the exponent 3.5 is a power, not a multiplier.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the power 3 only. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 2.
That multiplies 2 by 3.5. The exponent is a power, so 2 is raised to it.

questions.prompt: Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find the main-sequence lifetime of a 0.5 M☉ red dwarf in billions of years, to one decimal place.
hints: A negative power of one half is a positive power of two.
Work out 2²·⁵.
Multiply by 10 billion years.
questions.onCorrect: 56.6 billion years. A negative power flips 0.5 to 2, so the lifetime grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That raises 0.5 to +2.5. The power is negative, which flips it to 2²·⁵.

questions.prompt: Taking the mass boundaries from the last screen, what remnant does a star of initial mass 15 M☉ leave? Answer in two words.
hints: Its core collapses in a supernova but stops short of a black hole.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A neutron star. Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova that leaves a neutron star.

questions.onCorrect: A neutron star. Stars of about 10 to 40 M☉ end in a core-collapse supernova.

misconceptions.feedback: Black holes need still heavier stars. At 15 M☉ the core collapses but stops short.
White dwarfs come from stars below about 10 M☉. This star is heavier.

questions.prompt: A star spends 10 million years on the main sequence. Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find its mass in solar masses, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide the lifetime by 10 billion years to get M⁻²·⁵.
Invert to get M²·⁵.
Raise 1,000 to the power 1/2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 16 M☉. Invert the rule: M is t ÷ 10 billion years raised to the power −1/2.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is M²·⁵. Raise it to the power 1/2.5 to get M.
That divides by 2.5. A power of 1/2.5 is a root, not a division.

questions.prompt: What will the Sun become after its red-giant stage?
hints: Compare the Sun's mass with the boundary for a supernova.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At 1 M☉ the Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary. It will shed its outer layers and leave a carbon-oxygen white dwarf about the size of Earth.

questions.onCorrect: A white dwarf. The Sun is well below the 10 M☉ boundary, so it sheds its outer layers.

misconceptions.feedback: Neutron stars come from stars of about 10 to 40 M☉. The Sun is far lighter.
Black holes need still heavier stars. The Sun is well below the boundary.

questions.prompt: Star X has 3 times the fuel of star Y and burns it 12 times as fast. How long does X's fuel last compared with Y's? Give a decimal.
hints: Lasting time is fuel divided by burn rate.
Take Y's fuel and rate as 1, so X's are 3 and 12.
Divide 3 by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lifetime = fuel ÷ burn rate = 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 of Y's.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. X has more fuel, but it burns so much faster that the fuel lasts a quarter as long.

misconceptions.feedback: That is upside down. More fuel lengthens the life and a faster burn shortens it.
That multiplies fuel and rate. Fuel lengthens the time and burn rate shortens it, so divide.

questions.prompt: A star has more mass than the Sun. How does its main-sequence life compare?
hints: Compare how fast fuel and burn rate grow with mass.
questions.onCorrect: Burn rate grows much faster than fuel, so heavier stars live shorter lives.

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel, yes, but the burn rate grows far faster. The burn rate wins.
Burn rate depends strongly on mass, so lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent in M⁻²·⁵ negative?
hints: Divide M by M³·⁵.

acceptedIdeas: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.

choices.label: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
Mass is measured in solar units.

questions.onCorrect: M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵: the burn rate outgrows the fuel, so the lifetime shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign has nothing to do with size. It comes from dividing M by M³·⁵.
Solar units set the scale, not the sign of the exponent.

questions.prompt: Using L ∝ M³·⁵, how many times the Sun's luminosity does a 10 M☉ main-sequence star have? Give the nearest hundred.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 10³·⁵ into 10³ × 10⁰·⁵.
Multiply 1,000 by √10, then round to the nearest hundred.
questions.onCorrect: 3,200 L☉. A tenfold mass gives thousands of times the light.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 10 by 3.5. The exponent is a power applied to 10.
That is 10³. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 10.
